3: Implement an evaluator for a very simple subset of Forth.

5: [Forth][forth]
6: is a stack-based programming language.
7: Implement a very basic evaluator for a small subset of Forth.
8: 
9: Your evaluator has to support the following words:
10: 
11: - `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` (integer arithmetic)
12: - `DUP`, `DROP`, `SWAP`, `OVER` (stack manipulation)
13: 
14: Your evaluator also has to support defining new words using the customary syntax: `: word-name definition ;`.
15: 
16: To keep things simple the only data type you need to support is signed integers of at least 16 bits size.
17: 
18: You should use the following rules for the syntax: a number is a sequence of one or more (ASCII) digits, a word is a sequence of one or more letters, digits, symbols or punctuation that is not a number.
19: (Forth probably uses slightly different rules, but this is close enough.)
20: 
21: Words are case-insensitive.

## Summary

I implemented the Forth evaluator in `forth.go` (the only file changed). The design:

- **`Forth(input []string) ([]int, error)`** — iterates over each line, tokenizing with `strings.Fields`. On encountering `:` it parses a definition (`: name body ;`), rejecting numeric names as illegal; otherwise it executes each token.

- **`inline`** — the key subtlety. When a word is defined, any user-defined words in its body are expanded into their *current* definitions. This captures meaning at definition time, which the tests require: `: foo 5 ; : bar foo ; : foo 6 ; bar foo` yields `[5, 6]`, and `: foo 10 ; : foo foo 1 + ; foo` yields `[11]`. Since bodies are fully inlined at creation, execution never recurses into the dictionary and can't loop.

- **`execToken` / `execBuiltin`** — numbers are pushed; user-defined words run their inlined body; built-ins implement `+ - * / dup drop swap over` with stack-underflow and divide-by-zero errors. All lookups go through `strings.ToLower`, making everything case-insensitive.

- **`isNumber`** — matches an optional leading `-` plus one or more ASCII digits, so `-1` is a number but `-` is the subtraction operator.

Error cases return a non-nil error (the tests only check error presence, not message), and successful runs return the stack as a slice — `[]int{}` for an emptied stack, so `reflect.DeepEqual` matches the expected `[]int{}`.
